title: John Sweller's Cognitive Load Theory (1988)
explainer: Educational psychologist John Sweller's 1988 theory distinguishes cognitive load that's inherent to the material being learned from 'extraneous' load created purely by how information is presented, such as forcing a reader to flip back and forth between a diagram and a separate block of explanatory text (the split-attention effect). For technical writing, this is a concrete, testable argument for practices like labeling a diagram directly instead of placing a legend beside it, and for preferring worked examples over asking a reader to puzzle through a brand-new concept unaided.

title: Rudolf Flesch's Readability Formula (1948)
explainer: In 1948, Rudolf Flesch published a regression formula, the Flesch Reading Ease score, that predicts how hard a passage is to read using only two measurable quantities: average sentence length and average syllables per word. It's a simple, mechanical example of turning a fuzzy quality judgment, 'is this clear?', into a scorable number, and the same formula, later extended with psychologist J. Peter Kincaid into the Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level for the U.S. Navy in 1975, still ships inside the readability checkers in Microsoft Word and Grammarly today.
